scenes.say: How does a maze solver know the exit is exactly eight steps away, without trying every route? By the end, you'll do that, and order tasks with prerequisites, using the same two traversals.
Today we'll do three things. Find the shortest way out of a maze. Count islands on a grid. Then order tasks that depend on each other.
lines: Shortest way out of a maze: BFS.
Count islands on a grid: DFS.
Order tasks that depend on each other.

scenes.title: Shortest way out
scenes.statement: A 5×5 maze: a dot is floor, a hash is a wall. Moving up, down, left or right, what is the fewest steps from top left to bottom right?
scenes.note: Moves: up, down, left, right. Never through a wall.
scenes.say: You're standing top left in a five by five maze, and the exit is bottom right. Fewest steps? The answer is eight. Moves: up, down, left, right. Never through a wall.

scenes.head: Two ways to explore
scenes.say: A graph is nodes joined by edges. A grid is one: each cell touches four neighbors. Two ways to explore. Breadth first search spreads like ripples in a pond, nearest first, using a queue. Depth first search follows one tunnel to its end, then backs up.

scenes.head: BFS: ripples through a maze
scenes.say: Here's a maze. Dots are floor, hash marks are walls. You start top left. The exit is bottom right. Breadth first search spreads like ripples. Layer zero is the start. Layer one. Layer two. Layer three has two cells, because the path forks. Layer four. Layer five has three. Layer six. Layer seven. Layer eight reaches the exit. Eight steps.

scenes.head: BFS: set the stage
scenes.say: Three things. The grid, with hash for a wall. A distance table, filled with minus one, which means not visited yet. And a queue, first in, first out. Start at the top left: distance zero, and into the queue. The four directions are down, up, right, left.

scenes.head: BFS: the loop
scenes.say: Now the loop. While the queue has cells, pop the front one. Try its four neighbors. Skip any that fall off the grid. Skip walls, and skip cells already visited. Otherwise the neighbor is one step further: set its distance, and queue it. Every cell enters once, so the cost is O of rows times columns. The answer is d of four, four: eight.
Your turn. We knock out the wall right below the start. Does the exit get closer? What's its distance now? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Wall under the start removed. Exit distance?

scenes.head: Still eight
scenes.say: Eight. Knock out that wall and the left column gets closer: two, three, four. The bottom row gets closer too: five, six, seven. But the exit stays at eight. On a five by five grid you need four steps down and four across. Walls only add distance, never remove it.

scenes.head: Three BFS mistakes
scenes.say: Three mistakes. Marking visited on pop, not push: cells enter the queue many times. Checking the wall before the bounds: you read outside the grid. Using depth first search for fewest steps: you get a path, not the shortest.

scenes.title: Count the islands
scenes.statement: A grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water). Land touching up, down, left or right forms one island. How many islands?
scenes.say: Look at this grid of ones and zeros. Touching ones form an island, so how many islands? Three. Touching means up, down, left, or right.

scenes.head: One tunnel at a time
scenes.say: Picture a maze and a ball of string. Follow one tunnel to the very end. Dead end? Back up to the last fork, and try the other way. That's depth first search. The backing up is recursion, or a stack.

scenes.head: Counting islands
scenes.say: A grid of ones and zeros. Touching ones, up, down, left, or right, form an island. Scan in order. The first one, top left, starts island one. Sink it: depth first search turns it and every touching one to zero. Keep scanning. The next one starts island two. Sink those three. The lone corner one is island three. Sink it too. Answer: three.

scenes.head: DFS: sink an island
scenes.say: Here's the depth first search. If the cell is off the grid, or not a one, stop. Otherwise sink it: set it to zero. Then visit the four neighbors, down, up, right, left. Each call goes one cell deeper before the others get a turn. The recursion is the backing up.

scenes.head: Scan the grid
scenes.say: Now the scan. For every cell, if it's a one, we found a new island. Count it, then sink the whole island with the search. Every cell is visited at most once, so the cost is O of rows times columns. On our grid it prints three.
Your turn. Same grid, but now diagonal neighbors count as touching. How many islands? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Same grid, diagonals now count as touching. Islands?

scenes.head: Diagonals merge islands
scenes.say: Two. The corner one touches the middle island at a corner, so with diagonals they become one. Up, down, left, right keeps them apart. To allow diagonals, loop over eight directions instead of four.

scenes.head: BFS or DFS?
scenes.say: Which one? Fewest steps: breadth first search, a queue. How many areas, or can I reach it: depth first search. Very deep grid? Recursion can overflow, so use an explicit stack. Cost for both: O of V plus E, nodes plus edges.

scenes.title: Order the courses
scenes.statement: Some courses need others first. Give an order where every prerequisite comes before the course that needs it, or say it is impossible.
scenes.note: A loop of prerequisites makes it impossible.
scenes.say: Four courses with rules. Zero before one and two, both before three. One valid order is zero, one, two, three. A loop makes it impossible.

scenes.head: Getting dressed
scenes.say: Think about getting dressed. Socks must come before shoes. Pants must come before shoes, too. Many orders work, but shoes never come first. Finding any such order is a topological sort.

scenes.head: Kahn's algorithm: peel what's ready
scenes.say: Courses zero to three. An arrow means take this first. The box beside each course counts its unfinished prerequisites. Only a course with zero is ready. Zero is ready. Take it. Its two arrows vanish, so one and two drop to zero. Take one. Course three drops to one. Take two. Now three drops to zero. Take three.

scenes.head: Kahn: count and seed
scenes.say: First, count the arrows pointing into each course: its indegree. Here g of u lists the courses that need u. Then queue every course with indegree zero. Those are the ones ready to take.

scenes.head: Kahn: peel and repeat
scenes.say: Then loop. Pop a course and add it to the order. For each course that needs it, remove one prerequisite. If that reaches zero, it's ready, so queue it. At the end, fewer than n courses in the order means some never became ready. That's a cycle. Time is O of V plus E: each course and arrow is touched once.
Your turn. Four courses. Zero before one, zero before two, one before three, two before three. Which order is valid? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Many valid orders
scenes.say: Zero, two, one, three is valid. Zero goes first, because nothing precedes it. Two goes next: its only prerequisite, zero, is done. Then one, for the same reason. Three comes last, after both. One and two can swap, since neither needs the other. So several orders are valid, and Kahn's queue picks one.

scenes.head: A cycle has no valid order
scenes.say: Now add one more arrow: three to zero. Course zero waits on three. Look at the boxes. Every course has an unfinished prerequisite. No box says zero, so the queue starts empty. Nothing can start. The order stays empty, shorter than four. That's a cycle: they all wait on each other.

scenes.head: Both cases, end to end
scenes.say: Here it is end to end. With our four arrows, the order is zero, one, two, three. Then we add the arrow from three to zero, and call again. Zero of four courses finish. Fewer than n means a cycle.

scenes.head: When they push further
scenes.say: Follow ups. Alphabetically smallest order? Use a min heap instead of the queue. Another way? D F S: add a node after its children, then reverse. Classic problems: LeetCode two oh seven, two ten, and two sixty nine. Common mistake: never comparing the order size with n.
rows: never comparing order size to n

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do they work? B F S: queue, layers. D F S: stack, depth. Shortest path? B F S, if unweighted. Cost? O of V plus E. Deep recursion crashes? Use an explicit stack.
rows: How do BFS and DFS work?
BFS: queue, layers · DFS: stack, deep

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a topological sort? An order where every prerequisite comes first. How do you compute it? Kahn: queue indegree zero, pop, decrement. Detect a cycle? The order is shorter than n. Cost? O of V plus E.

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these three next. LeetCode two hundred, number of islands: depth first search. LeetCode ten ninety one, shortest path in binary matrix: breadth first search. LeetCode two oh seven, course schedule: Kahn's cycle check.
rows: LeetCode 1091 · Shortest Path in Binary Matrix

scenes.say: So say this. Breadth first search: a queue, fewest steps. Depth first: areas. Mark cells when you push. Both cost O of V plus E. Kahn's queue peels indegree zero. A short order means a cycle.
lines: BFS: queue, fewest steps. Both cost O(V + E).
DFS: areas. Mark cells when you push.
Kahn: indegree zero first. Short order = cycle.
